primary_content.text: In late 2023, the Thailand Elite Visa was officially rebranded as the Thailand Privilege Visa. While the name has changed to the Thailand Privilege Visa, the core benefit remains the same: it is the only program that grants a guaranteed 5, 10, 15, or 20-year renewable residency visa for Thailand.

As an authorized General Sales and Services Agent (GSSA) for the Thailand Privilege Card, Siam Legal provides free, fast-track processing for this program. Whether you are a digital nomad, retiree, or investor, this guide covers the new 2026 Thailand Privilege Visa membership tiers, prices, and benefits.

primary_content.text: To qualify for the Thailand Privilege Card membership program, you will need to meet the following eligibility requirements:
Hold a valid foreign passport with at least 1 year of remaining validity
No record of significant visa overstays in Thailand
No criminal history, bankruptcy proceedings, or mental incompetence
Must not currently hold or previously have held a Thailand Volunteer Visa
Note: Education Visa holders may apply for a Thailand Elite Visa but must submit additional verification documents.

main_topic.main_title: The Thailand Elite Visa is Now the Thailand Privilege Visa
main_topic.author: Rex Baay

primary_content.text: Once you’ve met all of the above, you will need to gather the following documents for your Thailand Elite Visa application:
Completed Membership Application Form
Color scan of passport biodata page
Proof of relationship documents for family applicants
Education Visa Acknowledgement Form (if applicable)
Siam Legal ensures all documentation meets Thailand Privilege Card Co., Ltd.'s requirements before submission.

main_topic.main_title: The Thailand Elite Visa is Now the Thailand Privilege Visa
main_topic.author: Rex Baay

primary_content.text: Before applying, it is recommended to consult a government-partnered General Sales and Services Agent (GSSA). GSSAs provide free assistance in helping you complete your application for the Thailand Privilege Card.
Here are the steps to take when applying for a Thailand Privilege Visa:
Submit a copy of your passport and application form. Ensure your passport has at least 1 year of validity remaining.
We also recommend scanning pages in color; black and white scans are often rejected, causing delays for your Thailand Privilege Visa.
Thai Immigration performs a criminal background check. This is the longest part of the wait. We monitor this status daily to ensure no files are lost during the Thailand Elite Visa processing.

You receive an approval letter and an invoice. You pay the fee directly to Thailand Privilege Card Co., Ltd. Payment can be made by card, mobile banking, bank transfer, Alipay, or cash. Cryptocurrency is also accepted, but must be arranged through a GSSA.
You can have the Thailand Privilege Visa affixed at the airport, a Thai embassy abroad, or the Immigration Bureau in Bangkok. We help clients choose the fastest option.

main_topic.main_title: The Thailand Elite Visa is Now the Thailand Privilege Visa

primary_content.text: Members who are already residing in Thailand on a short-term tourist visa or a standard visa exemption stamp can complete the physical visa attachment locally instead of traveling abroad.

This office handles the legal conversion from a temporary entry stamp to the long-term Privilege Entry Visa. On the day of your appointment, bring your physical passport along with the documents submitted at booking.

Non-Immigrant Visa Holders: If you hold an active Non-Immigrant visa (such as a Business, Marriage, or Retirement visa), it must be cancelled before your Privilege Entry sticker can be affixed. Cancellation must take place at the immigration office that originally issued the visa. If that office is outside Bangkok, the cancellation must be arranged in advance to cover your appointment date, since Chaeng Watthana does not accept same-day cancellations, nor cancellations processed under a 7-day extension.

Active Overstay Status: If you have an active overstay record, the office will not process the affixation under any circumstances until the overstay is fully cleared, the penalty fine is paid, and a clean, fresh entry is executed back into Thailand.

primary_content.text: If you have concerns about the 2026 tax residency rules, previous visa overstays, or clearing the mandatory government background check, ask our Senior Immigration Consultant directly.

With over 16 years of experience specializing in Thai immigration and more than 2,000 successful visa approvals, Rex Baay has helped clients navigate straightforward applications as well as complex immigration matters. Here are some of the questions he is asked most often.

main_topic.h_title: Can I apply if I currently hold another Visa?
main_topic.main_title: The Thailand Elite Visa is Now the Thailand Privilege Visa
main_topic.author: Rex Baay

primary_content.text: Yes. You can apply for the Thailand Privilege Visa while holding another valid Thai visa, such as a Retirement, Non-Immigrant O, ED, or Non-Immigrant B visa. If your current visa is still valid when you're ready to have your Thailand Privilege Visa affixed, it will need to be cancelled first, usually at the office where it was originally issued. Our team will review your situation and guide you through the easiest pathway, ensuring a smooth transition at every step.

main_topic.h_title: What documents do I need to prepare for visa affixation?
main_topic.main_title: The Thailand Elite Visa is Now the Thailand Privilege Visa
main_topic.author: Rex Baay

primary_content.text: The requirements depend on where you choose to have your Thailand Privilege Visa affixed. If you're affixing your visa at the airport, we recommend bringing recent bank statements showing your financial means and, if applicable, proof of employment, as immigration officers may request these at their discretion. Simply answer any questions honestly and demonstrate your genuine intention to stay in Thailand under the terms of the Thailand Privilege Visa. If you're affixing your visa at the Chaengwattana Immigration Office in Bangkok, you'll need a valid TM30 receipt, a Thai phone number, and your latest entry stamp so we can arrange your appointment. Our team will coordinate the appointment process on your behalf to ensure everything goes smoothly.

main_topic.h_title: Can I upgrade after my membership ends?
main_topic.main_title: The Thailand Elite Visa is Now the Thailand Privilege Visa
main_topic.author: Rex Baay

primary_content.text: Yes. When your membership expires, you have two main options: you can repurchase a new Thailand Privilege membership based on the packages available at that time, or you can upgrade to a higher-tier membership, such as from Bronze to Platinum. Upgrading requires payment of the applicable upgrade fee along with the price difference between the two membership packages. You will then have access to the added benefits and Privilege Points that come with the higher membership package.

main_topic.h_title: Do I need Health Insurance to be Eligible to apply?
main_topic.main_title: The Thailand Elite Visa is Now the Thailand Privilege Visa
main_topic.author: Rex Baay

primary_content.text: No. Health insurance is not required to apply for the Thailand Privilege Visa. Unlike many long-term visa options, there are no minimum income, employment, or age requirements, making the application process simple and accessible for most applicants. With very little paperwork involved, you'll only need to complete and sign the application forms, provide a copy of your passport and a passport-sized photo, and our team will take care of the entire application submission on your behalf, guiding you through each step of the process.

main_topic.h_title: Will the Thailand Privilege Visa make me a Thai tax resident under the 2026 tax residency rules?
main_topic.main_title: The Thailand Elite Visa is Now the Thailand Privilege Visa
main_topic.author: Rex Baay

primary_content.text: No, the visa itself carries no tax residency status. Residency depends on your physical presence in Thailand and how foreign-sourced income may be treated when remitted into Thailand under the current tax rules. If you're relocating with meaningful overseas income, this is the point where many people receive expensive advice that turns out to be incomplete or incorrect. That's why we offer clients a complimentary consultation with our in-house tax advisors to review your residency exposure before you commit to a move date, not after.

main_topic.h_title: What is the 180-Day Tax Rule for Thailand Privilege Visa holders?
main_topic.main_title: The Thailand Elite Visa is Now the Thailand Privilege Visa
main_topic.author: Rex Baay

primary_content.text: If you're physically present in Thailand for 180 days or more in a calendar year, you're generally treated as a Thai tax resident, regardless of which visa you hold. That status may bring foreign-sourced income within the scope of Thai taxation under the current rules. The actual exposure depends heavily on your income sources, any applicable tax treaty, and how funds are transferred into Thailand. This is one area where "it depends" is genuinely true, and where a short consultation can prevent a costly assumption.

primary_content.text: The visa program is fully active, but it is no longer branded as "Thailand Elite Visa." It now operates under the name Thailand Privilege Visa. While the branding has changed, the core benefits remain the same, including long-term visa options ranging from 5 to 20 years.

The key difference is flexibility. Under the former Thailand Elite Visa program, membership packages offered a fixed set of benefits. The Thailand Privilege Visa introduces a Points System, allowing members to customize their experience (e.g., redeeming points for flights or health checkups).
Yes. As with the old Thailand Elite Visa, you do not need a re-entry permit, you can open a Thai bank account easily, and you get access to the Elite Personal Liaison for 90-day reporting.

No. You must resolve any overstay and leave the country before applying; the Thailand Privilege application does not grant a visa extension or forgive an existing overstay. A history of overstays, particularly more than one or two within the past few years, can also affect approval of a new application even after the overstay itself has been resolved. Speak with our team before applying if you have any overstay history, so we can assess your situation first.

Tourist Visa, Visa on Arrival, or visa exemption: You can apply normally. If you are already in Thailand and your current entry is still valid, your Privilege Entry Visa can typically be affixed at the Immigration Bureau in Bangkok.

Non-Immigrant Visa (e.g., Non-B work visa, Non-O marriage visa, Non-OA retirement visa): Thai immigration law only allows one active visa type at a time, so your existing non-immigrant visa must be cancelled before your Privilege Entry Visa can be activated. Our team will walk you through this cancellation step so there is no gap in your legal status.

Education (ED) Visa: You may still apply, but additional verification documents are required. As long as you can provide proof that you genuinely attended classes, most cases are approved. Note that your ED Visa must also be cancelled before the Privilege Entry Visa can be activated, if it is still valid at that time.

primary_content.text: Your Privilege Entry Visa will be issued to match your passport's remaining validity rather than the full 5-year visa term. For example, if your passport expires in 2 years, your visa will be valid for that same 2-year period rather than 5 years. When you renew your passport, the remaining validity of your membership can be transferred to the new passport. We can coordinate with the TPC team on this transfer for you.

No. The Privilege Entry Visa is classified as a tourist visa, so it does not permit you to apply for a Thai work permit or take up local employment. You can still be a shareholder (up to 49%, the legal limit for foreign ownership) or director of a Thai company without a work permit, and there are no restrictions on remote work performed for an employer or clients based outside Thailand. If you need to work legally for a Thai company, you can obtain a separate Non-Immigrant B visa and work permit. Your Privilege membership will remain active and continue running, but your visa will switch to the work visa instead.

TM30 is a long-standing Thai immigration requirement under which a landlord, hotel, or property owner must report a foreigner's stay at their address within 24 hours of arrival. It applies to all foreigners in Thailand, including Thailand Privilege members, and responsibility for filing it rests with the host rather than the visa holder. You may still be asked to present a TM30 receipt when completing your 90-day report or other immigration procedures, so it's worth confirming with your landlord or hotel that it has been filed. We generally only need the TM30 to request your visa affixation appointment at the Chaengwattana Immigration Office, and in some cases, we can help issue it on your behalf if you provide your landlord's ID and blue book.

Each entry under the Privilege Entry Visa permits a stay of up to one year before an extension is required if you do not leave and re-enter the country. Failing to extend on time before the entry stamp expires can result in an overstay, which carries the same daily fine that applies to any overstay in Thailand regardless of visa type, and may affect future applications or renewals. Your annual extension booking is handled by Member Service, and our team can coordinate with them on your behalf. We recommend scheduling your extension well before the expiry date to avoid any risk of overstay.
